newsitem.title: SPAIN: Peseta volatility may last, but weakness won't.
newsitem.headline: Peseta volatility may last, but weakness won't.

text.p: The Spanish peseta is unlikely to go into freefall on European single currency nerves, but it may be jumpier as the selection of which countries will be in the launch approaches, analysts said on Tuesday.

"The peseta's fall is temporary, but we believe this year will bring many situations like this as new doubts emerge over Spain's participation in monetary union," said Fernando Mazon, analyst at Adisa Catalunya.

The peseta hit 85.20 to the mark on Monday, its lowest rate since August, after comments from financial leaders doubting whether Italy, Spain and Portugal would make the first phase of European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Last week Jurgen Stark, a senior figure at Germany's Finance Ministry, said simply fulfilling EMU targets was not good enough and that some countries would have to prove they were stable enough to join.

On Monday, a top German banker followed up, calling for a smaller group of countries to start the single currency project. He said the debate on whether Spain or Italy should be included was unsettling financial markets.
After weakening to 85.20 against the mark on Monday, the peseta managed to recover some ground by 1400 GMT on Tuesday to 84.80 to the mark with help from the Bank of Spain, dealers said.
Analysts said the markets' slide after days of comments by financial leaders questioning the likelihood of Spain's participation from the start of EMU was not surprising.
But they did not expect the drop to continue, saying strong economic fundamentals would provide a tonic for the financial markets.
Spanish Budget Secretary Jose Folgado said on Tuesday that the fall in the peseta and bonds on Monday did not reflect Spain's economic health, and analysts agreed.

"While inflation is falling, the current account is in surplus and the deficit nears three percent of GDP (gross domestic product). Episodes such as those we've seen in the past few days should be, in principle, transitory," said Cesar Cantalapiedra, economist at Analistas Financieros Internacionales.
He said a depreciation of the peseta to above 85 to the mark should not cause alarm.
"Nobody's bothered whether the peseta is at 84 or 85, but they are if it falls at a rate of 0.25 (of a peseta) per day, and that's what the Bank of Spain is there to avoid" he said.
He added that the central bank has enough foreign currency reserves to curb brusque movements in the peseta.

The Bank of Spain said on Tuesday its forex reserves rose $3.46 billion to $65.29 billion in January. Since the start of 1996, the bank's coffers have swelled by 70 percent, mostly because of foreign exchange intervention to stop the peseta from appreciating excessively, as was the case for much of last year.

For this reason, analysts said the peseta's slide from 83.30 to the mark in mid-January to 84.80, seen as a big move in a short time, should please both the central bank and the politicians who are keen to keep Spanish exports competitive.
"It's not surprising the peseta has weakened from 83.30, a level where (it) is clearly overvalued," said one economist who sees the peseta eventually settling around 85.50 to the mark.

But Antonio Villarroya, economist at Merrill Lynch in Madrid, predicts this recent decline is just the beginning of the volatility. This year will see the markets see-saw according to the prevailing mood of Euro-optimism or pessimism, he said.
"If we know for certain we'll be part of monetary union, the risk premium (of 10-year bonos over Bunds) will fall to 60 basis points, and if we are excluded, it will rise to 200," he said.
But Villarroya said the only really negative aspect of increased peseta volatility might be the implied delay in the next cut in interest rates from the current 6.00 percent.
